clinicalPearls: The classic nephritic picture is gross haematuria (often described as tea- or cola-coloured urine), oedema, and hypertension.
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is the most common cause in children and typically follows a group A streptococcal throat infection by about 1-2 weeks or a skin infection by 3-6 weeks.
Although labelled non-infective as a glomerular process, it is an immune-mediated sequela of a preceding streptococcal infection rather than active kidney infection.
Look for evidence of recent streptococcal infection with elevated antibody titres (such as ASO) and a low serum C3 that typically normalises within 6-8 weeks.
Fluid overload from sodium and water retention can precipitate hypertension, pulmonary oedema, and hypertensive encephalopathy.
Urinalysis characteristically shows red blood cells, red cell casts, and mild to moderate proteinuria.
Management is largely supportive with salt and fluid restriction and control of hypertension; the condition is generally self-limiting in children.
Persistently low complement beyond 8 weeks should prompt consideration of an alternative diagnosis such as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis or lupus nephritis.
reference.pathophysiology: Immune complexes involving streptococcal antigens deposit in or form within the glomerular basement membrane, activating the complement cascade (predominantly the alternative pathway). This drives glomerular inflammation with endothelial and mesangial proliferation and neutrophil influx, reducing the glomerular filtration surface. The result is a fall in filtration rate, sodium and water retention, haematuria, and proteinuria producing the nephritic syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Alport syndrome or thin basement membrane disease
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and microscopy for red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells
Evidence of streptococcal infection (ASO, anti-DNase B, throat or skin swab)
Renal biopsy if the course is atypical, complement stays low, or renal function deteriorates
redFlags: Severe hypertension or hypertensive encephalopathy (headache, seizures, altered consciousness)
Pulmonary oedema or respiratory distress from volume overload
Rapidly rising creatinine suggesting rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
Oligoanuria or features of acute kidney injury requiring dialysis
reference.prognosis: The great majority of children with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis recover completely, with resolution of gross haematuria within weeks and normalisation of complement within about two months; microscopic haematuria may persist for a year or more. A small minority develop chronic kidney impairment.
pitfalls: Assuming all paediatric nephritis is post-streptococcal and missing lupus or membranoproliferative disease when complement stays persistently low
Overlooking hypertension, which may be asymptomatic yet dangerous, by not measuring blood pressure
Fluid overloading a child with impaired filtration
Attributing dark urine to dehydration rather than examining the urine sediment
management: Antibiotic eradication of residual group A streptococcal infection with penicillin, or a macrolide if penicillin-allergic
Sodium and fluid restriction to counter salt and water retention
Loop diuretics for oedema and fluid overload
Antihypertensive therapy such as calcium-channel blockers or vasodilators for hypertension
Urgent treatment of hypertensive encephalopathy and pulmonary oedema when fluid overload is severe
Monitor renal function, blood pressure, and urinalysis, with serial complement to confirm expected C3 normalisation
Paediatric nephrology referral and consideration of dialysis for severe or deteriorating renal impairment
Consider renal biopsy if the course is atypical or complement remains persistently low
